requirements.title: Source-statement boundaries and embedded-statement qualification
requirements.definition: A syntax term ending in -stmt follows the applicable source-form statement rules, including an end-of-line or semicolon boundary. A statement may carry a label except when it is part of another statement, as in the action of an IF statement or the assignment of a WHERE statement. The embedded action is not a separately labelable source statement. This convention is applied with the actual source-form continuation, comment, termination and label-position rules; it is not a claim that every physical newline ends a continued statement.

pending.statement-context-census: Needs an independently reviewed census connecting every -stmt production to its source-statement or embedded role and the applicable free/fixed source rules. Aggregate reviewed canonical boundary and labeling evidence without relabeling every positive statement example as an effect or universal diagnostic test. The current registry has no source-census evidence-case type.

requirements.oracle: S4_1_4_001_valid is one small free-form positive control. Ordinary assignments use newline and semicolon boundaries, an outer IF carries a legal label, and its assignment has no independent label. A WHERE statement similarly contains an unlabeled assignment with a defined one-element logical mask and same-shaped integer destination. Literal checks require scalar value 3 and array element 4, only to establish that these admitted statements are used.
requirements.oracle_limitation: Five finite admission facets share one program; they are not five independent executions or full effects. No fixed-form, all-statement, universal reporting, or comprehensive IF/WHERE semantics claim is made. No malformed embedded-label twin is manufactured. Canonical source-form tests retain their owners, and the complete statement-context census remains pending. Source-form violations engage 4.2 p2(5), which requires reporting capability, not mandatory fatal rejection.
requirements.dependencies: 6.3.2.4-.6 (PDF 72) governs the free-form control. 6.3.3.3-.5 (PDF 73) qualifies the general convention for fixed columns, continuation and labels. R515 (PDF 55-56), R1141/C1148/p2 (11.1.8.4, PDF 219), and R1042/R1046/R1047 plus 10.2.3.1 p2 and 10.2.3.2 p1/p12 (PDF 197-199) establish the embedded forms, equal array shapes and checked values. 6.2.5/R611/C603 permits the short nonzero label. Default integer values are small, and all data are defined before use. 6.4 p3 (PDF 73) explicitly keeps INCLUDE lines outside Fortran statements.

accounting.rationale: PDF 45 lines 22-25: separate the syntax-class naming convention, actual source restrictions, label permission and exception, and converse naming convention.

A -stmt class is interpreted using source-form statement rules. The genuine boundary restriction and embedded qualification are mapped separately, rather than relabeling the entire paragraph as a pure definition.
The end-of-line/semicolon restriction is interpreted with the canonical continuation and comment rules, not as mandatory termination at every physical record.
A source statement may be labeled, subject to the embedded exception and source-form-specific placement rules. No label is required merely because the production ends in -stmt.
The label permission excludes a statement that is part of another statement. Both source examples, IF and WHERE, are retained; their component actions do not gain independent source-statement labels.

PDF 45 lines 24-25: source-form statements are named with a -stmt suffix in the grammar. This is a document/source-census convention, not an extra executable S requirement. It does not turn INCLUDE lines into statements.
PDF 45 lines 26-27: two canonical grammar references, not two newly owned ordering or precedence effects.

Statement ordering is specified through program-unit/R502 and its expanded productions in 5.1 (PDF 53-56). This reference does not move those rules into 4.1.4 or independently close their source accounting.
Expression hierarchy is specified through expr/R1023 and its subordinate productions (10.1.2, PDF 168-171). No expression-precedence matrix is attributed to this cross-reference.
PDF 45 lines 28-29: accounts for the usual specifier meaning, attribute-specification use, and expressly nonexclusive other uses.
The -spec suffix convention covers specifiers, with input/output specifiers offered as an example. It is not itself a Fortran keyword or mandatory I/O operation.
The convention also covers declaration attribute specifications; array-spec/R814 (8.5.8.1, PDF 124) is the stated example. Its complete alternatives and semantics remain with its defining section.
The source explicitly allows a few other uses of -spec; the convention must not be converted into an exhaustive classification of productions.
PDF 45 lines 30-31: type-parameter naming convention and both canonical examples.
References to a type parameter together with its enclosing parentheses use the -selector suffix. This does not assert that every selector production has only a parenthesized alternative.

The source cites kind-selector/R706 (PDF 80) and length-selector/R722 (PDF 84). R722 also explicitly has an asterisk form, illustrating why this naming convention must not override concrete productions. Neither example introduces new local type-parameter requirements.

review_rationale: Independent source-first review and tested integration repairs: doc/source_audits/batch_006.json. Actual statement and embedded-context conventions retain their conditions. Finite controls do not establish the entire context census or justify blanket R/C invalid twins.
